intervention_label: CPX-351 (liposomal 5:1 cytarabine:daunorubicin) — origin of the fixed-ratio rationale
model_system: 15-cell-line in-vitro synergy panel plus murine leukemia xenograft efficacy models
n_units: 15 tumour cell lines in vitro; in-vivo group sizes not stated in the abstract
control_arm: free cytarabine:daunorubicin cocktail and liposomes at non-5:1 molar ratios
dose_and_schedule: liposome-encapsulated cytarabine:daunorubicin at varied molar ratios, sub-MTD daunorubicin component
mechanism: Co-encapsulation fixes the cytarabine:daunorubicin exposure ratio in plasma and marrow at 5:1, the ratio that was synergistic rather than antagonistic in vitro, so what the formulation controls is the ratio, not the total dose.
key_finding: A 5:1 molar ratio gave the widest synergy and least antagonism across 15 lines, and the liposome held that ratio in plasma for 24 hours. In vivo the 5:1 formulation had the best therapeutic index and produced long-term survivors that free-drug cocktails did not, with the advantage tracking prolonged maintenance of the synergistic ratio in bone marrow.
caveats: The rationale was built around ratio control in marrow of chemotherapy-naive animals. Nothing here bears on refractory disease, prior venetoclax exposure or extramedullary sites.

intervention_label: CPX-351 — marrow delivery and leukemia-cell uptake
model_system: CCRF-CEM bone marrow-engrafting leukemia xenograft in Rag2-M mice
control_arm: free cytarabine:daunorubicin cocktail; non-tumour-bearing marrow for the myelosuppression comparison
dose_and_schedule: repeat intravenous dosing of CPX-351 versus equivalent free-drug cocktail
mechanism: Liposomes are taken up intact by leukemia cells and release drug intracellularly, so the efficacy gain comes from marrow delivery and leukemic uptake rather than from any change to the two drugs.
key_finding: CPX-351 cleared marrow leukemia below detection for several weeks whereas the free-drug cocktail only transiently suppressed it, while myelosuppression in non-tumour-bearing marrow was similar for both. Drug concentrations in leukemia-laden marrow were markedly higher with CPX-351, and the first dose potentiated marrow accumulation of subsequent doses.
caveats: The leukemia-selective uptake claim rests on CCRF-CEM, a T-lymphoblastic line, not an AML model, and the mice were treatment-naive.

intervention_label: CPX-351 versus free drug against primary AML and normal progenitors
model_system: primary AML blasts and normal G-CSF-mobilised PB/BM cells in colony-forming and CD34+CD38- apoptosis assays
n_units: n=13 AML patients; n=7 normal donors
control_arm: free cytarabine:daunorubicin at the same 5:1 molar ratio
dose_and_schedule: 24-hour incubation across a concentration range, then CFC plating or flow cytometry
mechanism: The formulation widens the gap between leukemic and normal progenitor killing rather than raising absolute kill of leukemic cells, so what improves is therapeutic index, not potency against a resistant blast.
key_finding: Blasts and progenitors from patients who went on to achieve complete remission were more sensitive to both CPX-351 and free drug than the same cells from chemotherapy-refractory patients. Against AML colony-forming cells and CD34+CD38- blasts the liposome was no better than free drug at the same ratio; its advantage was a five-fold sparing of normal progenitors, matched by preferential intracellular accumulation in AML over normal cells.
caveats: In-vitro only with a 24-hour exposure, and refractoriness in this cohort was to conventional induction rather than to FLAG-IDA plus venetoclax.

intervention_label: CPX-351 — tissue distribution of encapsulated versus free drug
model_system: nonclinical PK/ADME species (rat and dog) without leukemia
control_arm: non-liposomal cytarabine/daunorubicin combination
dose_and_schedule: single-dose intravenous CPX-351 versus non-liposomal combination
mechanism: Encapsulation keeps both drugs inside liposomes while they circulate, so the free fraction available to partition into peripheral tissue falls even as total exposure lengthens.
key_finding: Tissue:plasma ratios for cytarabine and daunorubicin were generally below 1 after CPX-351 and above 1 after the non-liposomal combination, and unbound plasma and tissue concentrations were dramatically lower after CPX-351. Metabolite patterns and relative release of the two drugs were otherwise similar between formulations.
caveats: Healthy animals, no leukemia, no extramedullary lesion. Reading these data as a warning that a thigh chloroma sees less free drug from CPX-351 than from a conventional regimen is extrapolation from distribution, not a measured antitumour endpoint.

intervention_label: CPX-351 schedule and dose dependency in consolidation
exclusion_reason: Optimises consolidation scheduling in xenografts already at low disease burden. The question is remission induction at roughly 85% marrow blasts, and the induction pharmacology is carried by Tardi 2009 and Lim 2010 (Leuk Res).

intervention_label: CPX-351 against acute lymphoblastic leukemia xenografts
exclusion_reason: Pediatric Preclinical Testing Program ALL xenograft panel; disease lineage and age group both mismatched, and it adds nothing on AML remission induction.

intervention_label: Cladribine plus cytarabine — biochemical modulation underlying CLAG backbones
model_system: circulating AML blasts sampled during therapy, plus a cell-free human DNA polymerase alpha primer-extension assay
n_units: n=9 patients sampled; ara-CTP kinetics evaluable in 7
control_arm: each patient's own pre-cladribine ara-CTP accumulation rate; single agents in the polymerase assay
dose_and_schedule: ara-C 1 g/m2 over 2 h on day 1 and days 3-6; cladribine 12 mg/m2/day by continuous infusion for 5 days beginning 24 h after the first ara-C
mechanism: Cladribine inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and lowers competing dNTP pools, raising the rate at which blasts phosphorylate ara-C to its active triphosphate; tandem incorporation of CdAMP then ara-CMP by DNA polymerase alpha then stalls primer extension.
key_finding: Median rate of ara-CTP accumulation in circulating blasts rose about 40% after 24 hours of cladribine infusion in 7 of 9 patients. DNA synthetic capacity of those blasts fell further under the combination than under either drug alone and stayed suppressed until the next ara-C infusion.
caveats: A clinical PK/PD study read here for mechanism rather than a laboratory model. The patients were venetoclax-naive and blast burden was not analysed as a modifier of ara-CTP accumulation.

intervention_label: 225Ac-lintuzumab in venetoclax-resistant AML
model_system: venetoclax-resistant AML cell lines and two in-vivo AML xenograft models
control_arm: either agent alone and untreated controls
dose_and_schedule: 225Ac-lintuzumab combined with venetoclax; activities and schedule as published
mechanism: Alpha decay of 225Ac inside CD33-positive cells produces double-strand breaks whose repair burden depletes MCL-1, the protein carrying venetoclax resistance, so BCL-2 dependence is restored rather than bypassed.
key_finding: The combination killed venetoclax-resistant AML lines synergistically, with both double-strand-break induction and loss of MCL-1 protein. In venetoclax-resistant in-vivo models it gave significant tumour growth control and prolonged survival over either agent alone.
caveats: Sponsor-funded with Actinium employees among the authors. CD33 antigen density, unquantified in this patient, was not varied as a determinant of the effect, and the resistance models were line-derived rather than post-FLAG-IDA-plus-venetoclax.

intervention_label: CD33-directed immunoPET with matched ADC and 225Ac radioimmunotherapy arms
model_system: disseminated CD33-positive AML xenograft in mice with [64Cu]Cu-DOTA-anti-CD33 PET-CT and microCT co-registration
control_arm: non-leukemic mice for imaging; isotype and untreated controls for therapy arms
dose_and_schedule: [64Cu]Cu-DOTA-anti-CD33 for imaging; humanised anti-CD33 as ADC and as [225Ac]Ac-RIT for therapy
mechanism: CD33 is carried by most myeloid blasts, so one antibody both reports where disease sits and delivers payload to it; alpha emission then kills within a few cell diameters of the bound antibody.
key_finding: CD33 immunoPET detected AML at 95.65% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with signal concentrated in femur and tibia and highest in the epiphysis and metaphysis rather than spread evenly through the skeleton. The anti-CD33 ADC (P=0.02) and [225Ac]Ac-anti-CD33 RIT (P<0.00001) each cut disease burden against their controls.
caveats: Extramedullary detection is named as the unmet need, but the modelled disease was skeletal, so this does not establish that a CD33-directed radioconjugate reaches a soft-tissue chloroma.

intervention_label: 225Ac atomic nanogenerator platform (HuM195 and other internalising antibodies)
model_system: in-vitro panel including leukemia and lymphoma lines; in-vivo disseminated human lymphoma and solid prostate carcinoma xenografts
control_arm: unconjugated antibody and untreated animals
dose_and_schedule: single injections at kilobecquerel (nanocurie) levels in vivo; becquerel (picocurie) levels in vitro
mechanism: A single 225Ac atom carried inside the cell generates a cascade of four alpha emissions, and the clustered double-strand breaks that follow are the killing event, which is why the platform is pursued where cell-cycle-dependent and apoptosis-dependent drugs fail.
key_finding: 225Ac coupled to internalising antibodies killed leukemia, lymphoma, breast, ovarian, neuroblastoma and prostate lines at becquerel levels in vitro. Single nanocurie-level doses caused tumour regression and prolonged survival in disseminated lymphoma and solid prostate models without overt toxicity in a substantial fraction of animals.
caveats: The in-vivo arms were lymphoma and prostate, not AML; the AML in-vivo evidence for this platform sits in Garg 2021 and Srideshikan 2019. Independence of alpha lethality from p53 and cell-cycle position is a radiobiological premise of the platform, not something tested here.

intervention_label: 225Ac-HuM195 pharmacokinetics, dosimetry and toxicity in nonhuman primates
exclusion_reason: Healthy cynomolgus monkeys with no leukemia and no antileukemic endpoint. It bounds safety and dosimetry, not remission probability, which is what this question asks.

intervention_label: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin — CD33 saturation, internalisation and antigen re-expression
model_system: peripheral blood sampled during a phase 2 gemtuzumab study in relapsed AML, plus in-vitro binding and internalisation assays with confocal microscopy
control_arm: pre-infusion background saturation in the same patients; lymphocytes as a CD33-negative internal control
dose_and_schedule: samples taken immediately before and 3 and 6 h after the start of cycle 1 and cycle 2 infusions
mechanism: Gemtuzumab binds CD33, is internalised, and CD33 is continuously re-expressed at the membrane, so intracellular calicheamicin accumulates across repeated binding cycles instead of being capped by the surface antigen count at one moment.
key_finding: CD33 sites on blasts, monocytes and granulocytes were near-completely saturated within 3 to 6 hours of infusion, with no binding to lymphocytes. Saturation before cycle 2 exceeded pre-cycle-1 background because drug from the first cycle was still circulating, and pulse-labelling confirmed continuous CD33 re-expression driving further internalisation.
caveats: Relapsed but not post-allograft AML, and marrow blast burden was not analysed as a modifier of saturation, so this constrains rather than settles the antigen-sink concern at roughly 85% blasts.

intervention_label: Uproleselan (GMI-1271) — E-selectin blockade of vascular-niche chemoresistance
model_system: syngeneic mouse AML models including Sele-/- hosts, with human AML blast binding assays
control_arm: chemotherapy alone; wild-type versus Sele-/- hosts
dose_and_schedule: GMI-1271 (uproleselan) given with chemotherapy; schedule as published
mechanism: AML blasts release inflammatory mediators that raise endothelial E-selectin, and oncogenic changes in blast surface glycosylation increase binding to it; that binding signals through AKT and NF-kB to keep blasts alive through chemotherapy.
key_finding: Blasts with the highest E-selectin binding potential were 12-fold more likely to survive chemotherapy in vivo and were the main contributors to relapse. Removing E-selectin genetically or blocking it with GMI-1271 abolished the pro-survival signal, synergised with chemotherapy and doubled survival duration over chemotherapy alone while sparing normal HSC.
caveats: Survival duration rather than remission was the readout, and the models were chemotherapy-naive with no venetoclax exposure and no prior graft. GlycoMimetics funded part of the work and supplied the compound.

intervention_label: Marrow vascular leakiness and hypoxia as a burden-dependent determinant of chemotherapy response
model_system: AML patient-derived xenografts imaged by intravital two-photon microscopy, with patient marrow biopsies for validation
control_arm: non-engrafted mice; vehicle versus NO-synthesis inhibition
dose_and_schedule: NO synthesis inhibition given alongside induction-type chemotherapy in PDX
mechanism: Leukemic infiltration drives endothelial nitric oxide production, which makes marrow vessels leaky and the marrow hypoxic, and the same axis degrades the niche supporting residual normal HSC.
key_finding: PDX marrow vasculature was abnormally permeable and hypoxic, with nitric oxide identified as the mediator in both xenografts and patient biopsies. Induction chemotherapy that failed to restore normal vasculature carried a poor prognosis, and blocking NO production reduced permeability, preserved normal HSC function and improved treatment response in PDX.
caveats: Vascular abnormality tracked disease presence rather than being titrated against blast percentage, so it supports a burden-dependent mechanism without fixing a threshold.

intervention_label: Regional endosteal niche destruction by AML and its effect on chemotherapy efficacy
model_system: mouse AML models imaged by intravital microscopy of calvarium and long bone
control_arm: non-leukemic mice; chemotherapy alone versus chemotherapy plus deferoxamine
dose_and_schedule: deferoxamine or genetic endothelial rescue combined with chemotherapy
mechanism: Endosteal AML cells secrete pro-inflammatory, anti-angiogenic cytokines that dismantle the specific vascular compartment normal HSC depend on, so the damage is regional rather than uniform crowding.
key_finding: AML progressively degraded endosteal endothelium, stroma and osteoblastic cells while central marrow stayed vascularised and splenic vascular niches expanded, and remodelled endosteal regions lost the capacity to support non-leukemic HSC. Preserving endosteal endothelium with deferoxamine or genetically rescued HSC loss, improved chemotherapeutic efficacy and extended survival.
caveats: Mouse AML models, and the chemotherapy benefit required adding a niche-protective agent that forms no part of any regimen she is being offered.

intervention_label: Stanniocalcin 1 from AML-remodelled mesenchymal stroma as a block on normal haematopoiesis
model_system: humanised ex-vivo and in-vivo niche models combining primary AML cells, normal human HSPC and mesenchymal stromal cells
control_arm: HSPC with MSC but without AML; STC1 and HIF-1alpha knockouts
mechanism: AML transcriptionally remodels mesenchymal stromal cells, which then secrete stanniocalcin 1 under HIF-1alpha control; STC1 holds normal HSPC quiescent and blocks their differentiation without killing them.
key_finding: Normal HSPC in AML-infiltrated marrow stayed viable but quiescent and failed to differentiate, and the suppression was largely reproduced by MSC-derived secreted factors alone. Abrogating STC1 or HIF-1alpha relieved the block.
caveats: Gives a niche account of impaired blood-count recovery that persists while leukemia is present. The models did not test how quickly the block lifts after cytoreduction, which is what the count-recovery arm of an ELN CR actually depends on.

intervention_label: Adipocyte-niche collapse as the cause of failed myelo-erythroid maturation in AML
model_system: primary AML patient samples in co-culture with marrow stroma, and human AML xenografts in mice
control_arm: non-leukemic marrow co-cultures and non-engrafted mice; vehicle versus PPAR-gamma agonist
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo PPAR-gamma agonist administration; schedule as published
mechanism: AML suppresses marrow adipocytes, and loss of that adipocytic compartment unbalances regulation of residual normal HSPC so myelo-erythroid maturation stalls — a maturation failure rather than a space problem.
key_finding: Physical crowding by leukemic cells did not account for the marrow failure; disruption of the adipocytic niche did. PPAR-gamma agonists induced marrow adipogenesis, rescued healthy myelo-erythroid maturation and repressed leukemic growth at the same time.
caveats: Xenograft and co-culture only. Its bearing on this question is on why counts may not recover to ELN CR criteria even when blasts fall, not on which regimen to choose.

intervention_label: Endosteal quiescent leukemic stem cells surviving cytarabine
model_system: primary human AML xenografts in newborn NOD/SCID/IL2rg-null mice
control_arm: untreated engrafted mice; endosteal versus central marrow compartments
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo cytarabine, schedule as published
mechanism: Leukemic stem cells home to and engraft within the osteoblast-rich endosteal region and stay quiescent there, so a cell-cycle-dependent agent such as cytarabine has little to act on in the compartment that reseeds disease.
key_finding: Human LSC engrafted in the endosteal region were protected from chemotherapy-induced apoptosis while cycling blasts elsewhere were killed, and LSC exclusively recapitulated AML on serial transplantation. An LSC-specific transcriptional signature was stable across serial passages.
caveats: Chemotherapy-naive xenografts treated with single-agent cytarabine, and the work predates the venetoclax era, so it speaks to why deep marrow clearance is hard rather than to her specific sequence of failures.

intervention_label: AML-induced sympathetic neuropathy in the haematopoietic stem cell niche
exclusion_reason: Endpoints are leukemia progression and niche composition with no chemotherapy-response or remission readout. The niche-occupancy argument this question needs is carried by Passaro, Duarte and Waclawiczek.

intervention_label: Metabolic state of cytarabine-surviving AML cells (why the surviving clone is fitter)
model_system: AML patient-derived xenografts treated in vivo with cytarabine, plus high- and low-OXPHOS human AML cell lines
control_arm: vehicle-treated PDX; low-OXPHOS lines as the comparator
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo cytarabine on a clinically patterned schedule, with mitochondrial translation, electron transfer or fatty-acid oxidation inhibitors added
mechanism: Cells surviving cytarabine are not the quiescent immature LSC compartment but cells running high oxidative phosphorylation, high mitochondrial mass and CD36-driven fatty-acid oxidation; the metabolic state, not stemness, is what the drug fails to kill.
key_finding: AraC residual cells in PDX were enriched for neither immature nor quiescent cells nor LSC, but carried a high-OXPHOS signature that predicted treatment response in both PDX and patients. Forcing an energetic shift toward low OXPHOS restored cytarabine sensitivity.
caveats: First-exposure cytarabine in previously untreated PDX. No model here runs a second or third cytarabine-containing salvage, so applying it to her second salvage is directional rather than quantitative.

intervention_label: Clonal architecture of chemotherapy-treated AML relapse
model_system: paired diagnosis and relapse whole-genome sequencing of primary AML marrow with deep validation sequencing
n_units: n=8 patients, hundreds of somatic mutations validated
control_arm: each patient's own diagnostic sample as the reference clone
mechanism: Chemotherapy does not erase the founding clone; either that clone acquires further mutations or a pre-existing subclone survives and expands, so every treated relapse starts from a population already filtered for survival under the drugs just used.
key_finding: In all eight cases chemotherapy failed to eradicate the founding clone, and relapse followed one of two patterns: evolution of the founding clone, or expansion of a surviving subclone with added mutations. Relapse-specific mutations were enriched for transversions consistent with damage from the cytotoxic therapy itself.
caveats: Eight patients at first relapse with no second-salvage sampling. It grounds the selection argument for why later lines respond worse without measuring the size of that drop.

intervention_label: Mitochondrial apoptotic priming as the determinant of induction response
model_system: primary myeloblasts and normal HSC from AML patients profiled by BH3 profiling, correlated with clinical course
control_arm: normal HSC from the same profiling platform as the therapeutic-index comparator
mechanism: How close a cell's mitochondria already sit to the apoptotic threshold sets how much damage chemotherapy must inflict before death follows, and the gap in priming between myeloblasts and normal HSC is the physical basis of the therapeutic index.
key_finding: Priming measured by BH3 profiling predicted response to induction chemotherapy, relapse after remission and requirement for allogeneic transplantation, refining prediction beyond conventional biomarkers. The same profiling nominated BCL-2 inhibition as a targeted approach with a workable therapeutic index.
caveats: Newly diagnosed and relapsed patients from the pre-venetoclax era. Priming has not been measured in her disease and would need a fresh marrow sample to become actionable.

intervention_label: Acquired BAX loss after venetoclax and its effect on conventional chemotherapy sensitivity
model_system: patients relapsing after venetoclax-based therapy, AML cell lines under prolonged BCL-2 antagonist exposure, and BAX- or BAK-deficient model systems
control_arm: patients relapsing after genotoxic chemotherapy; BAK-deficient and parental cells
dose_and_schedule: prolonged in-vitro exposure to BCL-2 antagonists for the competition experiments
mechanism: Venetoclax selects for cells that have lost BAX, the effector that executes mitochondrial permeabilisation. Because BAX sits downstream of BCL-2 rather than alongside it, the loss blocks the apoptotic exit route itself rather than one input into it.
key_finding: Seventeen percent of patients relapsing after venetoclax-based therapy had acquired inactivating BAX mutations, which were rare after genotoxic chemotherapy, and BAX-mutant cells were competitively selected during prolonged BCL-2 antagonist exposure in vitro. BAX-deficient AML cells resisted BCL-2 targeting, but their sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy was variable rather than uniformly lost.
caveats: The variable chemotherapy sensitivity is the load-bearing detail for her: it argues against assuming blanket cross-resistance from venetoclax failure to a cytarabine backbone, and equally against assuming none. Most relapses sampled followed venetoclax plus azacitidine rather than venetoclax plus intensive chemotherapy.

intervention_label: Reduced global apoptotic priming as the common route to BH3-mimetic resistance
model_system: AML patient-derived xenografts with acquired resistance to venetoclax or the MCL-1 antagonist S63845, plus human clinical samples
control_arm: matched sensitive parental PDX; sequential versus concurrent BCL-2 and MCL-1 blockade
mechanism: Resistance to BH3 mimetics runs through a global fall in mitochondrial apoptotic priming caused by a shifting balance of BCL-2 family proteins, not through acquired mutations in leukemia genes. Blocking BCL-2 drives sequestered pro-apoptotic proteins onto MCL-1 and the reverse.
key_finding: Resistant PDX and patient samples had lower priming by BH3 profiling, with the responsible BCL-2 family alterations differing case to case. Dynamic BH3 profiling still identified agents that re-primed resistant myeloblasts, including FLT3 inhibitors and SMAC mimetics, and concurrent BCL-2 plus MCL-1 blockade outperformed sequential.
caveats: Cytarabine and anthracyclines were not among the agents re-profiled, so the step from lower global priming to a lower chance of chemotherapy-induced CR runs through Vo 2012 rather than through a direct test here.

intervention_label: Chemotherapy as a selective filter for pre-existing TP53-mutant clones
model_system: whole-genome sequencing of 22 therapy-related AML patients, deep sequencing of banked pre-treatment samples, and wild-type/Tp53+/- mouse bone marrow chimaeras
n_units: n=22 t-AML genomes; 4 cases with pre-treatment detection; mouse chimaeras as published
control_arm: de novo AML genomes; wild-type HSPC competing in the same chimaera
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo chemotherapy exposure of the chimaeras, agent and schedule as published
mechanism: Cytotoxic therapy does not create TP53 mutations. It removes the competition: TP53-mutant HSPC survive DNA damage that kills their wild-type neighbours and expand into the space.
key_finding: Mutation burden and chemotherapy-related transversion fraction were similar in t-AML and de novo AML, and the exact TP53 mutation found at diagnosis was already present at 0.003 to 0.7% years earlier, in two cases before any chemotherapy. In mouse chimaeras Tp53+/- HSPC preferentially expanded after chemotherapy exposure.
caveats: Her TP53 status is unresolved in both directions. The selection argument bears on why each successive cytotoxic line raises the odds that the surviving clone is TP53-aberrant, whichever way her 2019 and 2026 assays are eventually reconciled.

intervention_label: Dominant-negative effect of TP53 missense variants on the DNA-damage response
model_system: isogenic CRISPR-edited human leukemia cell lines carrying common TP53 missense variants, saturation mutational scanning of p53 single-amino-acid variants, and mouse competitive transplants under DNA damage
control_arm: isogenic TP53 wild-type and TP53-null lines; wild-type cells in the same mouse
mechanism: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domain act dominant-negatively over the remaining wild-type allele, so a single mutant allele blunts the p53 transcriptional response to DNA damage. No neomorphic gain of function was found.
key_finding: Functional, DNA-binding and transcriptional assays across the isogenic panel found loss of function with a dominant-negative effect and no gain-of-function activity. In mice that dominant-negative effect conferred a selective advantage to haematopoietic cells specifically on DNA damage, and AML patient outcomes gave no evidence of a separate gain-of-function penalty.
caveats: Cell lines and mouse chimaeras rather than AML PDX. It predicts blunted chemotherapy-induced apoptosis from a single missense allele, which matters directly if her 2019 pathogenic call is the true one.

intervention_label: DHODH inhibition plus hypomethylating agent as p53-independent cytoreduction
model_system: HMA-resistant TP53-mutated AML cell lines and mice bearing TP53-mutated AML
control_arm: parental HMA-sensitive cells; HMA alone; venetoclax; normal HSPC for the toxicity comparison
dose_and_schedule: teriflunomide scheduled the day before HMA versus same-day and day-after; intermittent metronomic dosing, with chronic dosing tested separately
mechanism: Hypomethylating agents are pyrimidine analogues that must outcompete endogenous pyrimidines to deplete DNMT1. Resistant and TP53-mutant cells raise CAD and pyrimidine pools; blocking DHODH with teriflunomide drops those pools, restores DNMT1 depletion, and cytoreduces through terminal differentiation instead of p53-dependent apoptosis.
key_finding: Venetoclax could not perform this role because BAX, a p53 target gene, was substantially lower in TP53-mutant than wild-type cells. Teriflunomide cut pyrimidine levels several-fold, restored DNMT1 depletion and cytoreduced HMA-resistant TP53-mutant AML while sparing normal HSPC; in mice the day-before schedule beat same-day and day-after, and chronic exposure reversed the benefit through compensatory salvage.
caveats: Differentiation-based cytoreduction is not the ELN CR endpoint this question asks about, and no in-vivo remission rate is reported. Schedule dependence is sharp enough that an off-protocol attempt could reproduce the resistance rather than the benefit.

intervention_label: EVI1-driven chemoresistance and T/NK-cell exhaustion in AML
model_system: KMT2A-MLLT1-transformed murine AML carrying an EVI1-promoter GFP reporter that separates Evi1-high from Evi1-low cells, with human AML expression datasets for validation
control_arm: Evi1-low cells from the same transformed population; shRNA controls
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo cytotoxic chemotherapy against sorted Evi1-high and Evi1-low populations
mechanism: EVI1 drives ERG and cyclin D1 as downstream effectors. ERG carries the aggressive, chemoresistant phenotype independently of stem-cell activity, while cyclin D1 turns on an IFN-gamma/STAT1 chemokine programme that exhausts T and NK cells.
key_finding: Evi1-high cells resisted cytotoxic chemotherapy and produced aggressive disease without extra stem-cell activity, and silencing Erg removed proliferation, chemoresistance and leukemogenic capacity together. Cyclin D1 produced an interferon signature with T- and NK-cell exhaustion that was mirrored in human AML datasets, and blocking IFN-gamma/STAT1 impaired EVI1-AML development.
caveats: A murine KMT2A-MLLT1 model with EVI1 overexpression rather than the 5-prime MECOM gain she carries. Neither ERG nor the IFN-gamma/STAT1 axis is druggable in a regimen deliverable within weeks, so the row explains her odds rather than changing her options.

intervention_label: Menin-MLL inhibition (VTP-50469) in KMT2A-rearranged leukemia
exclusion_reason: Menin-MLL inhibition depends on a KMT2A rearrangement or an NPM1 mutation keeping menin resident at target loci. Her lesion is KMT2A amplification at four copies with wild-type NPM1, so the mechanism has no substrate here.

intervention_label: Adipose-tissue niche as a chemotherapy sanctuary for CD36-positive leukemic stem cells
model_system: mouse blast-crisis CML model with gonadal adipose tissue engraftment, plus primary human blast-crisis CML and AML cells
control_arm: marrow-resident leukemic cells from the same animals; CD36-negative fraction
dose_and_schedule: in-vivo chemotherapy with paired assessment of marrow and adipose compartments
mechanism: A CD36-positive LSC subpopulation seeds adipose tissue, induces lipolysis there and burns the released fatty acids. The adipose microenvironment supplies both the fuel and the protection, so the same clone is harder to kill outside marrow than inside it.
key_finding: Adipose-resident LSC were protected from chemotherapy by the gonadal adipose microenvironment, and CD36-positive cells with distinctive metabolic properties were strikingly enriched there. CD36 marked a fraction of human blast-crisis CML and AML cells with the same behaviour.
caveats: Gonadal adipose tissue in a blast-crisis CML model, not a thigh myeloid sarcoma in AML. No preclinical model reports remission-induction rates for a myeloid sarcoma against any of her candidate regimens, so the sanctuary argument stays mechanistic.

intervention_label: Sinusoidal endothelial regeneration as the rate-limiting step for haematopoietic reconstitution
model_system: mice after chemotherapy, sublethal irradiation, or lethal irradiation rescued by bone marrow transplant, with conditional VEGFR2 deletion and antibody blockade
control_arm: untreated mice; VEGFR2-intact transplanted animals
dose_and_schedule: conditional VEGFR2 deletion in adults, or VEGFR2 blockade after lethal irradiation plus BMT
mechanism: Sinusoidal endothelial cells must regenerate through VEGFR2 signalling before transplanted HSPC can engraft and counts recover, so the vascular niche rather than stem-cell number is the rate-limiting structure.
key_finding: Chemotherapy and sublethal irradiation caused minor sinusoidal regression while lethal irradiation caused severe regression requiring transplantation to repair. Deleting or blocking VEGFR2 prevented sinusoidal reconstruction and, with it, engraftment and haematopoietic reconstitution.
caveats: Normal mice with no leukemia and no second-transplant model. It offers a structural reason why count recovery, the difference between CR and CRi, may lag in a marrow already conditioned once, without quantifying that six years post-allograft.
